lesson.title: Distance Vector Routing: Learning the Network by Talking to Your Neighbors
lesson.summary: Distance vector routing is a decentralized routing algorithm in which each router keeps a table of its best known distance to every destination and improves that table over time by comparing it with the distance vectors its directly connected neighbors advertise.
lesson.body:
In distance vector routing, no router ever gets a full map of the network. Instead, each router keeps a vector, a list, of its current best estimate of the distance, or cost, to every destination it knows about, and periodically sends that entire vector to each of its directly connected neighbors. When a router receives a neighbor's vector, it asks a simple question for every destination in it: if I sent traffic to that destination by going through this neighbor, would that be cheaper than what I am currently doing. If the answer is yes, the router updates its own table to route that way instead.

That update rule can be written precisely: a router x's estimated distance to destination y equals the minimum, over every neighbor v of x, of the cost to reach v directly plus whatever distance v itself has advertised to y. In other words, trust your neighbor's opinion about the rest of the network, add the cost of the hop to reach that neighbor, and see if it beats what you already believed. This rule, applied over and over as routers exchange updated vectors, is exactly the Bellman Ford idea explored formally in the next chapter.

A concrete example makes this click. Picture three routers, X, Y, and Z. X and Y are connected by a link of cost 2. Y and Z are connected by a link of cost 1. X and Z also have a direct link, but a poor one, at cost 7. Before any updates, each router only trusts its direct links: X's vector says distance 0 to itself, 2 to Y, and 7 to Z. Z's vector says 7 to X, 1 to Y, and 0 to itself. Now suppose Y sends its vector to X, and that vector says Y can reach Z at cost 1. X checks: going through Y would cost 2, to reach Y, plus 1, Y's cost to Z, for a total of 3, which beats the 7 X currently believes for its direct link to Z. X updates its table: distance to Z is now 3, next hop Y. By the same logic, once Z hears from Y that Y can reach X at cost 2, Z recalculates its own path to X as 1 plus 2, or 3, also beating its old direct cost of 7, and updates accordingly.

Notice what just happened: neither X nor Z needed to know anything about the other in detail, and neither needed a map of the whole network. Each one only needed its own direct link costs and whatever its neighbors chose to advertise, and from that limited, local information alone, the true shortest path, X to Y to Z, total cost 3, emerged after a couple of rounds of exchanges. That is the essential promise of distance vector routing: reasonably good, eventually correct paths, computed with only neighbor to neighbor gossip rather than global knowledge.
